title: World Court Says: Yes, Workers Have the Right to Strike!
summary: Have you ever heard of a strike? It’s when workers stop working together to demand better pay or conditions. Now, the world’s top court has said that striking is a protected right! On Thursday, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, Netherlands, gave an important opinion. It said that a big labor treaty from 1948—signed by 158 countries—covers the right to strike, even though the word “strike” never appears in it. The court’s 14 judges agreed that the freedom to join groups and protect workers’ interests includes walking off the job. This isn’t a law that countries must follow, but it carries a lot of weight. Labor unions were thrilled. Christy Hoffman, a union leader, said, “There is no right to organize without the right to strike!” The decision could affect labor rules and trade deals around the world. But the court also said that in some cases, the right to strike can be limited. For example, police or firefighters might have different rules. The United States is part of the International Labor Organization, which asked for this opinion, but it hasn’t agreed to the treaty. Still, the ruling gives workers a powerful tool if they face legal trouble for striking. It’s a big moment for workers everywhere!
why_it_matters: If you ever have a job someday, you might benefit from the right to join with coworkers to ask for better conditions — this court opinion helps protect that right for everyone.

keywords.explanation: When workers stop doing their jobs together to protest and ask for better pay or conditions.
A formal agreement between countries, like a contract that many nations sign.
The main court of the United Nations that settles disagreements between countries and gives legal advice.
An official view from a court that explains what the law means, but which is not a binding order.
A group that workers join so they can act together to protect their rights and improve their workplace.
The act of workers coming together as a group to speak with one voice about their jobs.

questions.question: What did the International Court of Justice say about the right to strike?
options: It is not a right at all
It is protected under the 1948 labor treaty
It is only allowed in the Netherlands
questions.correct_answer: It is protected under the 1948 labor treaty

options: They asked for strikes to be banned

Can be enforced by the police

It left the International Labor Organization

background_read: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the court of the United Nations, based in The Hague in the Netherlands, and it helps settle legal disputes between countries and gives advice on international rules.
The International Labor Organization (ILO) is a UN agency that sets worldwide standards for workers’ rights; it asked the court to clarify whether the right to strike was protected.

The 1948 treaty mentioned in the article is the Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise Convention. Even though it never uses the word ‘strike,’ the court said the right to strike is hidden in its meaning.
Article_Structure: WHO: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) and labor unions around the world.
WHAT: The court announced that a 1948 labor treaty includes the right to strike, even though the word ‘strike’ is not written in it.
WHERE: The decision was announced in The Hague, Netherlands, but it influences labor laws worldwide.
WHY: The International Labor Organization asked the court to settle a long debate, and the ruling gives workers a stronger legal argument when they strike.

perspectives.description: They see this as a huge victory because now they can point to an official world court opinion that says striking is a protected part of organizing.
Some might worry that more strikes could disrupt businesses, slow down important services, or hurt the economy.
Because the opinion is not a law, governments can still make rules about when and how workers can strike, especially for emergency jobs like police or firefighters.
